dryRun.title: Work done for different n (rounded)
dryRun.note: Look at the last row. When n grows 100,000 times, O(log n) only goes from 3 to 20, but O(n²) explodes. This gap is what Big O measures.

think.q:
let c = 0
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  for (let j = 0; j < 4; j++) c++
}
console.log(c)
why: The inner loop runs 4 times for each of the 4 outer rounds. Loops inside loops multiply: 4 × 4 = 16.
Trap: adding the two loops (4 + 4 = 8). That is the answer for loops one after the other.

think.q:
let c = 0
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) c++
for (let j = 0; j < 5; j++) c++
console.log(c)
why: Two loops one after the other add up: 5 + 5 = 10. In Big O this is still O(n), because 2n drops the constant.
Trap: multiplying (25). Multiplying is only for a loop inside another loop.
think.exec:
let c = 0
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) c++
for (let j = 0; j < 5; j++) c++
console.log(c)

think.q:
let n = 64, steps = 0
while (n > 1) {
  n = n / 2
  steps++
}
console.log(steps)
why: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. That is 6 halvings, and 6 is log₂(64).
Trap: thinking a loop over n always takes n steps. Cutting the input in half each time makes the work grow very slowly.

think.q: A function takes about 2 ms for n = 1,000 and about 8 ms for n = 2,000. Which growth fits best?
why: Doubling the input made the time four times bigger. That is the signature of O(n²): (2n)² = 4n².
Trap: O(2n) is not a separate growth. It is the same as O(n), and doubling n would only double the time.

think.q:
This function adds the numbers from 1 to n. It creates no arrays or objects.

function sum(n) {
  if (n === 0) return 0
  return n + sum(n - 1)
}

What is its extra space?
why: Each call waits for the next one, so n frames sit on the call stack at the deepest point. Space is O(n).
Trap: counting only variables you created. The call stack is memory too.

try.task: Write countHandshakes(n). At a party with n guests, every guest shakes hands with every other guest once. Count the handshakes with loops (do not use a formula), then say its Big O.
try.hint: For guest i, only count guests after i, so no pair is counted twice. That is a loop inside a loop.

takeaway.key: Big O tells you how the work grows as n grows, not how many seconds it takes.
mistakes: Keeping constants and small terms: O(3n + 10) is just O(n).
Adding when you should multiply: a loop inside a loop is n × n.
Forgetting space. Recursion uses stack memory even if you create no arrays.

dryRun.title: arr = [10, 20, 30], then arr.unshift(5)
dryRun.note: Every old element had to move. With n elements that is n moves, so unshift is O(n). push would have moved nothing.

think.q:
const a = [3, 1, 2]
const b = a.sort()
console.log(a === b)
why: sort changes the original array in place and returns that same array. So a and b are one array.
Trap: expecting a new sorted copy. Use [...a].sort() when you need to keep the original.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
const b = a.slice(1, 3)
console.log(a.length, b.length)
why: slice builds a new array from index 1 up to (not including) 3, so it has 2 items. The original keeps all 4.
Trap: thinking slice removes items. That is splice.

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
a.length = 1
a[3] = 9
console.log(a.length)
why: Setting length = 1 cuts the array to [1]. Writing at index 3 then makes length 4, because length is always the highest index plus one. Indexes 1 and 2 become empty holes.
Trap: thinking an array must stay packed. In JS it is an object with a length counter.

think.q: A loop calls arr.shift() n times to empty an array. Each shift moves every remaining element. Total time?
why: The moves are n + (n-1) + ... + 1, which adds up to about n²/2. That is O(n²).
Trap: reading one shift as O(1) because it is a single line of code.

think.q:
In a React component:

list.push(3)
setList(list)

The screen does not update. Why?
opts: push is too slow to update the screen
The array is the same object, so React sees no change
push returns a new array that is thrown away
why: push changes the array in place. React compares the old and new reference, finds the same one, and skips the update.
Fix: setList([...list, 3]) creates a new array.

try.task: Write rotateLeftOne(arr). Return a new array with the first item moved to the end. The original array must stay unchanged.
try.hint: slice(1) gives everything except the first item. Add arr[0] at the end.

checks.verify: const a = [1, 2, 3]; rotateLeftOne(a); assert(JSON.stringify(a) === "[1,2,3]", "input was changed")

takeaway.key: Work at the end of an array is cheap; work at the start or middle moves every element after it.
mistakes: Using shift or unshift inside a loop and getting O(n²).
Forgetting that sort, splice, reverse and push change the original.
Changing React state arrays in place instead of making a new array.

dryRun.title: Count letters in "banana" with a Map
dryRun.note: Step 4 is the key moment: the key already exists, so we update it. Each step is O(1), so the whole count is O(n).

think.q:
const m = new Map([[1, 'a']])
console.log(String(m.get('1')))
why: A Map keeps the key type. The number 1 and the string "1" are different keys, so get("1") finds nothing.
Trap: thinking Map turns keys into strings. A plain Object does that, a Map does not.

think.q:
const o = {}
o[1] = 'x'
o['1'] = 'y'
console.log(Object.keys(o).length)
why: Object keys are always strings. The number 1 becomes "1", so the second line overwrites the first.
This is the opposite of the Map in the question before.

think.q: console.log(new Set([{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }]).size)
why: A Set compares objects by reference, not by content. Two separate { a: 1 } literals are two different objects.
Numbers and strings are compared by value, so new Set([1, 1]).size is 1.

think.q:
const m = new Map()
m.set('a', 1)
m.set('b', 2)
m.set('a', 3)
console.log([...m.keys()].join(','))
why: Setting an existing key updates its value and keeps its original place in the order. So the keys stay a, b.
Trap: thinking the updated key moves to the end.
think.exec:
const m = new Map()
m.set('a', 1)
m.set('b', 2)
m.set('a', 3)
console.log([...m.keys()].join(','))

think.q: You must find out whether an array of n numbers has any repeated value, in O(n) time. Which is best?
opts: Two nested loops that compare every pair
Call includes() on a growing array inside one loop
Sort the array, then compare neighbours
Add each value to a Set, checking has() first
why: has() and add() are O(1) on average, so one pass is O(n).
Trap: includes() looks like one line but scans the array each time, so the loop becomes O(n²). Sorting works but costs O(n log n).

try.task: Write charCount(str). Return a plain object that tells how many times each character appears.
try.hint: Use a Map and update each count. At the end, Object.fromEntries(map) turns it into an object. Or use an object with (obj[ch] || 0) + 1.

checks.verify: const r = charCount("banana"); assert(r.b === 1 && r.a === 3 && r.n === 2, "wrong counts")

checks.t: empty string gives an empty object

checks.verify: const r = charCount("aA"); assert(r.a === 1 && r.A === 1, "a and A are different")

takeaway.key: Hash-based structures turn "search for it" into "look it up", which is O(1) on average.
mistakes: Calling includes() on an array inside a loop when a Set would do.
Using an Object when keys are not strings: the number 1 and the string "1" collide.
Expecting a Set to remove duplicate objects by content. It compares references.

dryRun.title: factorial(3)
dryRun.note: The stack grows to depth 3, hits the base case, then unwinds. The answer is built on the way back.

think.q:
function f(n) {
  if (n === 0) return 0
  return n + f(n - 1)
}
console.log(f(4))
why: Trap: 24 is 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. This function adds, it does not multiply.

think.q:
let out = ''
function show(n) {
  if (n === 0) return
  out += n
  show(n - 1)
  out += n
}
show(2)
console.log(out)
why: The first out += n runs on the way down (2, then 1). The second runs on the way back up (1, then 2). So the result is 2112.
Trap: forgetting that code after the recursive call runs during the unwind.
think.exec:
let out = ''
function show(n) {
  if (n === 0) return
  out += n
  show(n - 1)
  out += n
}
show(2)
console.log(out)

think.q:
function count(n) {
  return count(n - 1)
}
try { count(3) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: There is no base case, so the calls never stop. The stack fills up and JS throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
Every recursive function needs a path that returns without calling itself.

think.q: A recursive function sums an array of n numbers by calling itself with the next index. It creates no new arrays. What is its extra space?
why: The recursion goes n levels deep, and every level keeps a frame on the call stack. Space is O(depth) = O(n).
Trap: saying O(1) because no array is created.

think.q:
let calls = 0
function fib(n) {
  if (n === 2) calls++
  if (n < 2) return n
  return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
}
fib(5)
console.log(calls)
why: fib(2) is computed again and again by different branches of the call tree. Here it runs 3 times, just for n = 5.
This repeated work is why naive Fibonacci is O(2^n), and why memoization helps later.

try.task: Write sumDigits(n) with recursion. It returns the sum of the digits of a non-negative whole number.
try.hint: Base case: a single digit (n < 10) is its own sum. Otherwise take the last digit with n % 10 and recurse on Math.floor(n / 10).

takeaway.key: A recursive function needs a base case that stops it and a step that gets smaller; every waiting call costs stack space.
mistakes: No base case, or a base case the input never reaches.
Calling with an input that does not get smaller.
Forgetting return before the recursive call, so the result is lost.
Ignoring stack space: depth n means O(n) space.

dryRun.title: Two Sum: nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6
dryRun.note: At i = 0 we need 3 and the number is 3. If we stored it first, it would match itself. That is why we check first, then store.

think.q:
function twoSum(nums, target) {
  const seen = new Map()
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    seen.set(nums[i], i)
    const j = seen.get(target - nums[i])
    if (j !== undefined) return [j, i]
  }
}
console.log(twoSum([3, 2, 4], 6).join(","))
why: The code stores the number before looking for its partner. At i = 0 it finds itself (3 + 3 = 6) and returns [0, 0].
Fix: do the get first, then the set.

think.q:
const count = {}
for (const ch of 'aa') {
  count[ch] = count[ch] + 1
}
console.log(String(count.a))
why: The first time, count.a does not exist, so undefined + 1 is NaN. NaN plus 1 stays NaN.
Fix: start from zero with (count[ch] || 0) + 1.

think.q: Two Sum solved with a hash map, one pass. What are the time and extra space?
why: One pass with O(1) lookups is O(n) time. The map can hold up to n numbers, so space is O(n).
The O(n²) / O(1) option is the brute force. The map trades space for time.

think.q: You want to group words that are anagrams, such as "eat", "tea" and "ate". Which key puts them in the same group?
why: All anagrams have the same letters, so sorting the letters gives one shared key: "aet".
Trap: "bat" and "bar" share a first letter and "eat" and "bat" share a length, but they are not anagrams.

think.q:
const m = new Map()
m.set({}, 1)
console.log(String(m.get({})))
why: Object keys are matched by reference. The second {} is a different object, so nothing is found.
Use strings or numbers as keys when you want lookups by value.

try.task: Write firstUnique(str). Return the first character that appears only once in the string, or null if there is none.
try.hint: Pass 1: count every character in a Map. Pass 2: walk the string again and return the first character whose count is 1. Two passes is still O(n).

takeaway.key: Ask "have I seen this before?" and let a hash map answer it in O(1) instead of scanning.
mistakes: Storing the current item before checking, so it matches itself.
Scanning an array inside a loop when a map would answer in O(1).
Using objects as keys and expecting lookup by content.
Forgetting that the map costs O(n) extra space.
